evaluation.positioning_hook: A hyper-ambitious college student time-traveling through trauma to save her mother discovers the real battle is learning how to live with grief, desire, and the stories she tells herself.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediately legible — a young woman time-traveling through her own trauma to save her mother — and it has clear emotional stakes. The audience is narrower than a four-quadrant genre play because the script leans heavily into psychology, theory, and interiority, but the mother-daughter engine gives it real reach.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast and keeps sharpening: Jessica starts seeing campus glitches, then discovers Henry, Maddox, and her mother are all tied into a shared temporal/psychic loop. The script repeatedly re-states the central engine through concrete set pieces — the steam tunnels, the yearbooks, the park, the hospital, the final bookstore frame — so the concept stays clear even as it gets stranger.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jessica is a strong lead because she’s brilliant, defensive, funny, horny, and emotionally blocked in ways that make her choices feel specific rather than generic. Henry and Maddox are also vivid counterweights — one needy and destabilized, one controlled and wounded — which gives the central triangle real heat.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: This is a very specific swing: campus horror, Lacanian theory, time travel, sexual politics, and maternal grief are fused into one voice. The script’s willingness to make the monster a psychic/trauma construct, then literalize it in multiple timelines, is unusually confident and distinctive.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps escalating through discoveries rather than repeating beats: campus haunting, 1999 travel, the mother reveal, the Henry/Maddox connection, the coma/hospital frame, and the final emotional resolution. There is some density and repetition in the middle as Jessica tests theories, but the set pieces keep the page turning.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea feels both strange and inevitable: a daughter’s grief manifests as time travel, and the men in her orbit become embodiments of the same wound. The final reveal that Jessica was her own babysitter, and that the story is really about becoming the author of her life, gives the premise a memorable emotional logic.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Morgan College, the steam tunnels, the frat house, the yearbooks, the campus gossip ecosystem, and the 1999/2002/2009/2014/2020s temporal layering all create a world with rules and texture. The setting is not just a backdrop; it generates the mystery, the social pressure, and the mythology.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually hard to imitate because it can pivot from raunchy campus comedy to metaphysical dread to sincere maternal catharsis without losing its voice. The script’s mix of smart-ass dialogue, academic jargon, and emotional sincerity is its own lane.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: On the surface this is a time-travel grief story, but underneath it’s about identity, authorship, inherited illness, sexual agency, and the stories families use to survive. The repeated motif of writing, revision, and memory suggests a lot of thematic depth beyond the immediate plot mechanics.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Jessica/Kerri is a strong friendship engine, Jessica/Henry is volatile and erotic, Jessica/Maddox is adversarial and therapeutic, and Jessica/Susan is the emotional spine. The supporting cast is not huge, but the relationships are rich enough that multiple pairings generate material.

lead_characters.name: Jessica Wolfe
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 19-20, college student; intellectually gifted, high-achieving, emotionally dysregulated, white, upper-middle-class American.
lead_characters.hook: Jessica is a hyper-competent overachiever who uses wit, intellect, and control to outrun grief, then gets pulled into a time-bending confrontation with her mother’s death, her own desire, and the stories she’s built to survive. She’s funny, prickly, self-aware, and increasingly vulnerable as the script strips away her defenses and forces her to become the author of her own life.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Saoirse Ronan in Lady Bird or Carey Mulligan in Promising Young Woman — a role that lets an actor play intelligence, rage, comedy, sexuality, and breakdown in the same performance. It’s a full-spectrum lead with big emotional turns, sharp dialogue, and a final catharsis that would reset how people see the actor.

lead_characters.name: William Maddox
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s-60s, college professor; white, intellectually formidable, emotionally guarded, married/divorced depending on timeline.
lead_characters.hook: Maddox is the brilliant, manipulative, grief-stricken professor who becomes Jessica’s guide, antagonist, and emotional mirror across timelines. He’s seductive in the way authority can be seductive, but the script keeps revealing the loneliness and guilt underneath the performance of certainty.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Paul Giamatti in Sideways — a role built on intelligence, menace, woundedness, and the ability to make long speeches feel like emotional combat. It gives an actor a rare chance to play both the intellectual gatekeeper and the broken father trying to redeem himself.

lead_characters.name: Henry Maddox
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late teens/early 20s, college student; white, mentally unstable, charismatic, sexually needy, suicidal.
lead_characters.hook: Henry is the damaged, magnetic son whose need for connection curdles into obsession, self-destruction, and temporal haunting. He’s funny and pathetic and dangerous in equal measure, which makes him feel like both a romantic lead and a warning sign.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Timothée Chalamet in Beautiful Boy or Robert Pattinson in The Lighthouse — a role where fragility, charm, volatility, and menace all live in the same body. It’s the kind of part that lets a young actor go from cute to terrifying without changing costumes.

lead_characters.name: Susan Wolfe
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 20s-30s in flashbacks; Jessica’s mother; white, impulsive, brilliant, unstable, deeply loving.
lead_characters.hook: Susan is the emotional center of the story: the mother whose illness, vitality, and impossible love shape Jessica’s entire inner life. She’s not just a victim or a symbol; the script gives her wit, sexuality, defiance, and a heartbreaking insistence on choosing her own life.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Toni Collette in Hereditary or Laura Linney in The Savages — a role that asks for warmth, volatility, humor, and devastating emotional truth. It gives an actor the rare chance to make a mother feel mythic without losing her humanity.

lead_characters.name: Kerri
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 19-20, college student; Jessica’s best friend, socially fluent, blunt, loyal.
lead_characters.hook: Kerri is the grounded best friend who can puncture Jessica’s self-mythologizing while still being the person who shows up when it matters. She’s the script’s pressure-release valve and moral reality check, but she also has enough bite to feel like a real person, not a sidekick.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Beanie Feldstein in Booksmart or Auli’i Cravalho in The Power — a role that lets an actor be funny, loyal, and emotionally essential without being ornamental. It’s a great friend part with real comic timing and a few sharp dramatic turns.

lead_characters.name: Donovan de Vries
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 19-20, college student; awkward, intelligent, socially anxious, white.
lead_characters.hook: Donovan is the campus outsider whose obsession with theory and performance art makes him both useful and embarrassing to Jessica. He’s a little pathetic, a little sincere, and exactly the kind of guy who can accidentally unlock the plot while trying to impress the wrong person.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jesse Eisenberg in The Squid and the Whale or Michael Cera in Superbad — a role that lets an actor play awkward intelligence, romantic humiliation, and comic self-awareness. It’s a strong supporting part for someone who can make cringe feel human.

lead_characters.name: Nancy
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 20s-30s in the story’s internal logic; Black woman, imagined/recurring figure tied to memory and caregiving.
lead_characters.hook: Nancy begins as Jessica’s invented confidante and becomes one of the story’s most emotionally clarifying figures, embodying care, memory, and the possibility of unconditional love. She’s both a narrative device and a deeply felt emotional presence, which gives her unusual weight for a supporting role.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Regina Hall in Support the Girls or Janelle Monáe in Hidden Figures — a role that can be warm, funny, and quietly authoritative all at once. It gives an actor the chance to play the kind of presence that changes the emotional temperature of every scene.

lead_characters.name: Gary Wolfe
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s-50s, Jessica’s father; physician, loving, exhausted, practical.
lead_characters.hook: Gary is the steady parent trying to manage a crisis he doesn’t fully understand while still protecting his daughter from herself. He’s not flashy, but the script gives him real tenderness and the kind of weary authority that makes the family scenes land.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jeffrey Wright in The Farewell or Kyle Chandler in Friday Night Lights — a role built on quiet emotional authority, restraint, and the pain of being the parent who can’t fix everything. It’s a strong father part with real dignity.

lead_characters.name: Chloe Maddox
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 40s-50s, Henry’s mother; warm, needy, socially awkward, emotionally porous.
lead_characters.hook: Chloe is the mother who loves too much, needs too much, and accidentally helps create the conditions for Henry’s collapse. She’s comic, sad, and unsettling in a way that makes the family system feel lived-in rather than schematic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Patricia Clarkson in Pieces of April or Catherine O’Hara in Schitt’s Creek — a role that lets an actor play warmth, neediness, and denial with real specificity. It’s a juicy mother part that can swing from funny to tragic in a beat.

lead_characters.name: Erica
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s-40s, Susan’s friend; adult, sober, emotionally open, grounded.
lead_characters.hook: Erica is the adult witness who can actually tell Jessica what her mother was like before the illness took over. She’s a small role, but she carries crucial memory and gives the story a lived-in social history.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Amy Ryan in Gone Baby Gone — a role that can do a lot with a little, especially in scenes where memory, guilt, and affection all collide. It’s a great character part for an actor who can make exposition feel personal.

lead_characters.name: Rob
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 20s, college athlete; easygoing, socially confident, physically imposing but kind.
lead_characters.hook: Rob is the clean contrast to Henry: uncomplicated, decent, and present, which makes Jessica’s encounter with him feel like a test of whether she can inhabit her own body without spiraling. He’s not a plot engine so much as a relational mirror.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Glen Powell in Everybody Wants Some!! — a role that lets an actor be charming, funny, and physically relaxed without turning into a cliché jock. It’s a deceptively useful part because it makes the lead’s emotional state legible.

casting_characteristics: multiple age versions of the same characters
child versions of Jessica, Susan, and Henry
one lead role with heavy emotional and comedic range

locations.period_or_contemporary: contemporary with extensive 1999, 2002, 2004, 2009, and 2014 period sequences
notable_requirements: college campus with dorms, lecture halls, steam tunnels, and frat house
New Hampshire and Los Angeles period looks

technical.vfx_details: time-slip transitions, reality overlays, black-monster manifestations, temporal morphs, and a few crowd/appearance continuity effects
technical.sfx_needs: practical blood, gunshot aftermath, fire effects, hospital chaos, and monster-enhancement work

rights_flags.detail: Penderecki’s 'Threnody to the Victims of Hiroshima' is plot-critical and repeatedly named.
Shirley Bassey’s cover of 'Light My Fire' is specifically used in a key sex sequence.
The Doors' 'Light My Fire' is referenced through the cover performance and may require clearance depending on use.
The Beatles are plot-relevant in the John Lennon murder sequence and related dialogue.
Twilight is prominently referenced as a childhood reading object.
Prius is repeatedly used as a specific family vehicle reference.
AOL is specifically named in Maddox’s email correspondence.
Disneyland, Starbucks-like campus culture references, and other named consumer/cultural brands appear in dialogue and setting texture.
John Lennon assassination depiction and the Dakota shooting sequence invoke real historical figures and events.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release; best positioned as a prestige genre title with awards-adjacent and specialty theatrical potential

budget.note: Contemporary campus and house interiors keep the base manageable, but the period jumps, hospital sequences, monster effects, and multiple time-era recreations will push above a simple contained indie.

casting.note: Jessica has to carry comedy, erotic tension, breakdown, and philosophical dialogue; Henry and Maddox both need actors who can play charisma and menace without flattening the material. Child casting continuity across Jessica/Susan/Henry is also load-bearing.

development.note: The script has a strong internal logic, but the dense theory language, repeated timeline resets, and ambiguity around what is literal versus psychological will be a buyer conversation point.

comp_set.why_it_comps: A grief monster that externalizes trauma while staying emotionally specific, with the parent-child wound driving the horror language.

comp_set.title: Palm Springs
comp_set.why_it_comps: A time-loop premise used to explore emotional avoidance, relationship repetition, and the comedy of being trapped in your own pattern.

comp_set.why_it_comps: Memory, love, and identity are treated as a surreal emotional puzzle rather than a clean genre mechanism.

comp_set.why_it_comps: A young woman’s self-invention, romantic drift, and fear of choosing the wrong life are the emotional spine.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like smart, emotionally literate genre films where the premise is strange but the feelings are painfully recognizable.
audience_target.demographics: 18-44 skewing female, with strong appeal to college-educated viewers, prestige-genre audiences, and viewers drawn to grief/identity stories.

budget_tier.note: Campus locations, period recreations, child casting, and moderate VFX keep this above micro, but it remains fundamentally a contained character-driven feature.

types_of_buyers: director-driven buyers looking for awards-capable material
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where genre is used as a delivery system for grief, identity, and emotional catharsis. The script’s intellectual confidence and contained production footprint make it attractive to buyers who want something distinctive without tentpole scale.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The story resolves as a closed emotional arc, and there is no clear franchise or spinoff vector beyond the core Jessica/Henry/Maddox triangle.

strengths.what_it_means: This gives the film a commercial hook that is more than a gimmick: the sci-fi premise is inseparable from the emotional wound. Buyers can sell it as a concept movie with real feeling, which broadens the lane beyond pure genre fans.
strengths.evidence: The black monster, the time slips, and the final hospital/house convergence all trace back to Jessica’s mother’s death and her inability to process it.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Jessica is a star-making lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The part has the kind of contradiction that attracts name actresses and can launch a younger one: smart, funny, horny, defensive, and emotionally wrecked. That makes the project packaging-friendly because the lead is a genuine draw, not just a vessel for plot.
strengths.evidence: Her campus banter, breakdowns with Maddox, sexual scenes with Rob and Henry, and final catharsis all ask for different registers.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script has a clean conceptual spine.
strengths.what_it_means: The buyer can understand the movie in one sentence, which is a real advantage in a crowded market. The premise is weird, but the rules are consistent enough to support a confident pitch and a memorable trailer.
strengths.evidence: The campus glitches, yearbook clues, steam tunnels, and repeated time jumps all point to the same central mechanism.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The mother-daughter relationship is the emotional moat.
strengths.what_it_means: This is what keeps the movie from feeling like a clever puzzle only. It gives the project a cross-demographic emotional entry point that can reach viewers who don’t usually buy high-concept sci-fi.
strengths.evidence: The final 2004 maternity ward scene and the repeated longing to see Susan as a living person rather than a wound.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world is specific enough to market.
strengths.what_it_means: Morgan College, the steam tunnels, the frat house, and the campus rumor mill create a memorable setting that can be sold visually and tonally. That specificity helps the movie stand out from generic time-travel or trauma dramas.
strengths.evidence: The yearbooks, Discord/chat chatter, dorm party culture, and New Hampshire college texture.

strengths.what_it_means: This is the kind of material that can attract a director with taste and an actor looking for a showcase, while still being contained enough to finance. That combination is valuable because it lowers the dependency on IP while preserving upside.
strengths.evidence: Contained locations, strong lead role, and a concept that plays as both emotional drama and elevated sci-fi.

whats_special.headline: This is a smart, emotionally loaded elevated-genre feature with a real star role at its center and a premise that can be pitched in one breath. The contained college-world footprint, moderate VFX, and prestige-drama lane make it a credible buyer conversation for streamer originals, specialty distributors, or a director looking for a breakout feature.

items.area: The theory dialogue can narrow the audience.
items.detail: The Lacan/Freud/Schrödinger material is part of the script’s identity, but it also makes the movie feel more literate than accessible in stretches. Buyers will weigh whether the intellectual density is a feature or a barrier for the intended audience.

items.area: The middle section repeats the same emotional argument.
items.detail: Jessica cycles through several versions of the same question — is it real, is it trauma, can she save her mother — before the story fully cashes out. That repetition is thematically intentional, but it creates a development conversation about momentum and whether the audience will feel the loop as propulsion or drag.

items.area: The lead role is a demanding casting lift.
items.detail: Jessica has to play comedy, erotic charge, intellectual authority, panic, and grief without losing coherence. That narrows the pool to actors who can carry both prestige dialogue and genre intensity, which is a real packaging dependency.

items.area: The period jumps add production friction.
items.detail: The script moves through 1999, 2002, 2004, 2009, 2014, and 2020s material, which means wardrobe, vehicles, set dressing, and continuity all have to stay precise. It’s still manageable, but it’s not a simple contemporary shoot.

items.area: The rights and clearance list is not empty.
items.detail: Penderecki’s 'Threnody to the Victims of Hiroshima,' the Shirley Bassey/Doors music use, the Beatles/Lennon material, and the Twilight references all create real clearance and budget conversations. None of that kills the project, but it does mean the music and historical-reference plan needs to be handled deliberately.

items.area: The ending is emotionally satisfying but conceptually dense.
items.detail: The final resolution asks the audience to accept that the story is both literal and imagined, and that Jessica’s healing comes through authorship and grace. That’s elegant for the right buyer, but some commercial readers will flag the ambiguity as a risk if they want a cleaner genre payoff.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction is that its intelligence is also its filter: the theory-heavy dialogue and recursive structure will delight the right buyer while narrowing the casual audience. Production is still very doable, but the period layering, child casting, and music/history clearances mean this is a deliberate prestige-genre package, not a casual greenlight.
